lines: When we label word by word, the labels must fit together.
If every word picks its label alone, we can get O, then I person.
That is illegal. I must continue a name that already began.
So a good model also looks at the neighbouring labels.
The hidden Markov model does exactly that.
The tags are hidden. The words are what we see.
At each step it asks two questions. How likely is this tag after the previous tag? That is the transition.
And how likely is this tag to produce this word? That is the emission: the word given the tag, not the tag given the word.
Take two words: can fish. Each can be a noun or a verb. That gives four paths.
For each path, multiply the numbers along the way.
Verb then noun wins, with zero point one three four four.
This number is a joint probability. To get the posterior, divide by the total of all four paths.
With long sentences, there are far too many paths to try.
The Viterbi algorithm keeps, for every tag, only the best way to reach it.
Viterbi takes the maximum. The forward algorithm takes the sum, which gives the total.
The CRF uses scores instead of probabilities.
A score can use any clue: a capital letter, a word ending, a list of names.
Add up the scores of a path, and divide by the total of all paths. That total is called Z.
But a CRF only prefers legal labels. To forbid illegal ones, we must block them.
For the exam:
The emission is the word given the tag.
A path product is joint. Divide by the total to get the posterior.
Viterbi uses the maximum. Z and the forward algorithm use the sum.
And entities are scored as whole spans, not word by word.
